answer: I can't give you the figure for the latest month with confidence: I have no live data access and my knowledge stops in the first half of 2026, while today is 10 October 2026. The latest report out now would normally be the one for September 2026, which I don't have. The last readings I recall, from memory, are about 4.3-4.4% in early 2026 (roughly 4.4% for February and 4.3% for March 2026), seasonally adjusted. My best estimate for now is somewhere in the low-to-mid 4% range. Source: U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics (Current Population Survey, Employment Situation report).

I can't confirm the latest month: I have no live data and my knowledge ends in the first half of 2026. As of 10 October 2026 the latest published figure would be for August 2026 (September's is due in mid-October), and I don't have it. The last readings I recall, from memory, are about 2.4% year over year for January 2026, then a rise to roughly 3% or a bit above in the spring of 2026 as energy prices went up. My best estimate for now is around 3%, but treat that as uncertain. Source: U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics (Consumer Price Index, CPI-U).

I can't give the latest month's figure reliably: my knowledge ends in the first half of 2026 and the most recent report as of 10 October 2026 would be for September 2026. The last figures I recall, from memory and subject to revision, are about +130,000 for January 2026, about -92,000 for February 2026 and about +178,000 for March 2026 (total nonfarm payrolls, seasonally adjusted). Job growth through that period was weak and volatile, so my best guess for a recent month is a change of well under 100,000 either side of the low tens of thousands. Source: U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics (Current Employment Statistics, Employment Situation report).

I don't have this week's figure: my knowledge ends in the first half of 2026 and the rate is published weekly (the latest would be for the week ending Thursday 8 October 2026). The last values I recall, from memory, are an average 30-year fixed rate of about 6.0% in February 2026, rising to about 6.3-6.4% in March-April 2026. My best estimate for now is around 6-6.5%. Source: Freddie Mac (Primary Mortgage Market Survey).

I can't give the latest daily value: my knowledge ends in the first half of 2026 and the most recent reading would be for 8 or 9 October 2026. The last levels I recall, from memory, are a 10-year Treasury yield of about 4.0-4.4% during the first months of 2026. My best estimate for now is in the low 4% range, but I can't confirm the exact value or date. Source: U.S. Department of the Treasury (daily par yield curve rates; also published by the Federal Reserve Board in its H.15 release).

The latest monthly figure would be for September 2026, which is beyond my knowledge (it ends in the first half of 2026). The last value I recall is a monthly effective federal funds rate of about 3.64% in early 2026 (January through at least March), with the target range at 3.50-3.75% after the December 2025 cut. If the Fed has not changed the target since then, it would still be about 3.6%; if it has cut again, it would be lower. I can't confirm which. Source: Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System (H.15 release; the daily rate is calculated by the Federal Reserve Bank of New York).

The most recent quarter reported as of 10 October 2026 would be Q2 2026 (third estimate, released in late September), and I don't have that figure; my knowledge ends in the first half of 2026. The last figures I recall, from memory, are real GDP growth at a seasonally adjusted annual rate of about 0.5-0.7% for Q4 2025 (after revisions) and about 2.0% for Q1 2026 (advance estimate). Treat the Q1 2026 figure as my best available answer, and note it has since been revised and superseded. Source: U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis.

I don't have the latest month: as of 10 October 2026 the most recent published figure would be for August 2026, and my knowledge ends in the first half of 2026. From memory, housing starts were running at roughly 1.3-1.5 million units at a seasonally adjusted annual rate in late 2025 and early 2026. My best estimate for now is about 1.4 million, but I can't confirm the exact figure. Source: U.S. Census Bureau and U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (New Residential Construction release).

I can't give the latest week: the most recent figure would be for the week ending 3 October 2026 (released 8 October), which is beyond my knowledge (it ends in the first half of 2026). From memory, seasonally adjusted initial claims were running at roughly 200,000-230,000 per week in early 2026. My best estimate for now is in or near that range, but I can't confirm it. Source: U.S. Department of Labor, Employment and Training Administration (Unemployment Insurance Weekly Claims report).

I don't have the latest reading: as of 10 October 2026 it would be the preliminary October 2026 or final September 2026 figure, and my knowledge ends in the first half of 2026. The last values I recall, from memory, are an index of about 56-57 in January-February 2026, about 53 in March 2026 and about 50 in April 2026, which was close to a record low. My best estimate for now is somewhere in the 50s, but that is uncertain. Source: University of Michigan, Surveys of Consumers.

About 14.8% (seasonally adjusted) for April 2020, per the Bureau of Labor Statistics (Current Population Survey). It was first reported as 14.7% and later revised to 14.8%. It is the highest rate in the monthly series, which goes back to 1948.
10.0% (seasonally adjusted) for October 2009, per the Bureau of Labor Statistics. This was the peak after the Great Recession. It was first reported as 10.2% and later revised to 10.0%.
About 18.63%, for the week ending October 9, 1981, per Freddie Mac's Primary Mortgage Market Survey. This is the all-time high for the weekly 30-year fixed average.

About 0.54% on March 9, 2020 (10-year constant maturity yield, daily close), per the U.S. Treasury Department, as also published in the Federal Reserve Board's H.15 release. This was a record low close at the time.

About 9.0% year over year in June 2022 on the seasonally adjusted CPI-U index, per the Bureau of Labor Statistics. The widely quoted headline figure of 9.1% uses the not seasonally adjusted index. The seasonally adjusted figure can shift by a tenth with annual seasonal factor revisions, so I am less sure of its last digit.

About 2.273 million units (2,273 thousand) at a seasonally adjusted annual rate in January 2006, per the U.S. Census Bureau and HUD (New Residential Construction). This was the peak of the 2000s housing boom.
50.0 (index, 1966:Q1 = 100) in June 2022, per the University of Michigan Surveys of Consumers. It was the lowest reading on record at the time.

About -$36.98 per barrel on April 20, 2020 (WTI spot at Cushing, Oklahoma), per the U.S. Energy Information Administration. The price was negative that day. The expiring May NYMEX futures contract settled at -$37.63 per barrel, which is the other commonly quoted figure.

Roughly 32% of disposable personal income in April 2020 (seasonally adjusted annual rate), per the Bureau of Economic Analysis. It is the record high for the series. It was first reported as about 33% and has been revised since; I believe the current figure is close to 32.0%, but I am unsure of the exact latest-vintage value.

About -28.0% at a seasonally adjusted annual rate in Q2 2020, per the Bureau of Economic Analysis, as currently revised to the best of my knowledge. The advance estimate was -32.9% and a later estimate was -31.4%; subsequent revisions moved it to roughly -28%. It is the steepest quarterly decline on record.
About 19.04% (monthly average effective federal funds rate, July 1981). Source: Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System (H.15). From memory, no lookup.

About $442,600 (median sales price of new houses sold, Q4 2022, not seasonally adjusted), as I recall the currently revised series. Earlier vintages showed higher figures (about $467,700 to $479,500) before revisions. Source: U.S. Census Bureau and HUD.

About 3.7% (the average of the 12 monthly seasonally adjusted rates for 2019 is roughly 3.67-3.68%; monthly values ranged from 4.0% in January to 3.5% in September). Source: U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, Current Population Survey.

5 months: January through May 2023 (roughly 6.3%, 6.0%, 5.0%, 5.0%, 4.1%). From June onward it was below 4%. May is the close call at about 4.1% on the seasonally adjusted index, so I am less sure of that month. Source: U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, CPI-U.
7.79%, for the week ending October 26, 2023 (30-year fixed-rate average, the highest since 2000). Source: Freddie Mac Primary Mortgage Market Survey.

My best answer is roughly 1.5 million jobs (December 2023 to December 2024, seasonally adjusted total nonfarm), on the data as revised by the benchmark published in early 2026. I am unsure of that exact figure. The number is heavily vintage-dependent: it was first reported as about 2.2 million and was about 2.0 million after the February 2025 benchmark. Source: U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, Current Employment Statistics.

About 130% (the not seasonally adjusted index rose from roughly 134.2 in January 2012 to roughly 308 in June 2022, i.e. about 2.3 times). The index levels are from memory, so the result could be off by a point or so. Source: S&P Dow Jones Indices (S&P CoreLogic Case-Shiller U.S. National Home Price Index).

About -1.08 percentage points (-108 basis points) on July 3, 2023, the deepest inversion since 1981. A near-equal low of about -1.07 occurred on March 8, 2023. Source: Federal Reserve Board H.15 / U.S. Treasury constant-maturity yields, with the spread calculated by the Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis.

3 quarters on currently revised data: 2020 Q1 (about -5.5%), 2020 Q2 (about -28%), and 2022 Q1 (about -1%). 2022 Q2 was originally reported as negative (-0.6%) but was revised to slightly positive in the 2024 annual revision, so older vintages would give 4. Source: U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis.

About 6.14 million (6,137,000, seasonally adjusted) for the week ending April 4, 2020, on the currently revised series. As originally reported, the peak was 6.87 million for the week ending March 28, 2020; later changes to the seasonal adjustment moved the peak. Source: U.S. Department of Labor, Employment and Training Administration.

First reported (BLS Employment Situation, April 4, 2025): total nonfarm payrolls rose by 228,000 in March 2025, seasonally adjusted. This was revised down to 185,000 and then to about 120,000 in the next two monthly reports. The February 2026 annual benchmark revision lowered 2025 job growth further (the March 2025 employment level was cut by roughly 900,000), so the current figure is below 120,000. I do not recall the exact post-benchmark number with confidence; my best estimate is somewhere under 100,000. Source: U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics (CES).

First reported (BLS, June 6, 2025): total nonfarm payrolls rose by 139,000 in May 2025, seasonally adjusted. This was revised to 144,000 and then sharply down to 19,000 in the August 1, 2025 report. The February 2026 benchmark revision changed it again; I do not recall the exact current figure, but my best answer is that it remains near zero, at or below roughly 19,000 and possibly slightly negative. Source: U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics (CES).

First reported (BLS, July 3, 2025): total nonfarm payrolls rose by 147,000 in June 2025, seasonally adjusted. This was revised to 14,000 and then to -13,000, a job loss, in the next two reports. The February 2026 benchmark revision changed it again; I do not recall the exact current figure, but my best answer is that it is still a small decline, around -13,000 or somewhat lower. Source: U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics (CES).

First reported (BLS, August 1, 2025): total nonfarm payrolls rose by 73,000 in July 2025, seasonally adjusted. This was revised to 79,000 and then to 72,000 in the next two reports. The February 2026 benchmark revision changed it again; I do not recall the exact current figure, but my best estimate is a modest gain of about 70,000 or somewhat less. Source: U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics (CES).

The advance estimate (BEA, April 28, 2022) showed real GDP falling at a 1.4% seasonally adjusted annual rate in Q1 2022. After later annual and comprehensive revisions, the current figure is about -1.0% annualized. It stood at -1.0% after the 2024 annual update and I believe it is unchanged or close to that after the September 2025 update, but I am not certain. Source: U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis.

The advance estimate (BEA, July 28, 2022) showed real GDP falling at a 0.9% seasonally adjusted annual rate in Q2 2022. Later revisions turned it positive: +0.3% annualized after the 2024 annual update, and I believe about +0.6% after the September 2025 annual update. I am not certain of the latest figure; my best answer is a small positive number between +0.3% and +0.6%. Source: U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis.

The advance estimate (BEA, January 30, 2025) showed real GDP growing at a 2.3% seasonally adjusted annual rate in Q4 2024. The third estimate was 2.4%. The September 2025 annual update revised it down to about 1.9%, which I believe is the current figure, though I am not certain it has not changed since. Source: U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis.

4.0%, seasonally adjusted, for January 2025. That was published in the BLS Employment Situation report of February 7, 2025; the February 2025 figure did not come out until March 7, 2025. Source: U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics (Current Population Survey).

About 159.5 million: 159,536 thousand, seasonally adjusted, for December 2024, as published in the BLS Employment Situation report of January 10, 2025 (a gain of 256,000 on the month). That was the figure on record on February 1, 2025; the benchmark revision released on February 7, 2025 then lowered the level. The exact thousands figure is from memory and could be slightly off. Source: U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics (CES).

As first reported (BLS, January 15, 2025), headline CPI-U for December 2024 was up about 2.9% from a year earlier. BLS's official 12-month figure is the not-seasonally-adjusted one, 2.9%; the seasonally adjusted index gave essentially the same 2.9%. The data now still show about 2.9%: the unadjusted figure is never revised, and the annual seasonal-factor revisions moved the adjusted index only by hundredths of a point (roughly 2.9% either way). Source: U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics.

The original source is Freddie Mac, from its Primary Mortgage Market Survey (PMMS). FRED carries it as the 30-Year Fixed Rate Mortgage Average in the United States (series MORTGAGE30US), in percent, not seasonally adjusted. It is published weekly, normally on Thursdays. The series goes back to April 1971.

The source is S&P Dow Jones Indices LLC. FRED's copy (series SP500, daily closing index level) only covers a rolling window of about the most recent 10 years, because of licensing limits, so as of October 2026 it would start around October 2016. It is not the full history of the index, and it is a price index that excludes dividends.

The source is S&P Dow Jones Indices LLC, which publishes it as the S&P CoreLogic Case-Shiller U.S. National Home Price Index (FRED series CSUSHPINSA, not seasonally adjusted, and CSUSHPISA, seasonally adjusted). It is a monthly index with January 2000 = 100. Note: the index branding may have changed recently (CoreLogic was rebranded as Cotality in 2025), so the current title on FRED may read differently; I am not certain of the exact present wording.

It comes from the University of Michigan's Surveys of Consumers. FRED carries it as University of Michigan: Consumer Sentiment (series UMCSENT), a monthly index with 1966:Q1 = 100, not seasonally adjusted. At the source's request, FRED shows it with a one-month delay.

The source is the U.S. Energy Information Administration (EIA). FRED carries it as Crude Oil Prices: West Texas Intermediate (WTI) - Cushing, Oklahoma (series DCOILWTICO), daily, in dollars per barrel, not seasonally adjusted, starting in January 1986.

The source is the U.S. Employment and Training Administration (ETA), part of the U.S. Department of Labor, from its weekly Unemployment Insurance Weekly Claims report. Yes, the headline series (Initial Claims, FRED series ICSA) is seasonally adjusted; it is weekly, in number of claims, for weeks ending Saturday. A not seasonally adjusted version (ICNSA) is also available.

FRED's headline real GDP series (GDPC1) is reported in billions of chained 2017 dollars, at a seasonally adjusted annual rate, quarterly. The source is the U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA). The reference year was 2017 as of my knowledge; BEA changes it at comprehensive revisions, so it is worth checking that it has not been updated since.

FRED's headline CPI-U series (CPIAUCSL, Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers: All Items in U.S. City Average) is an index with base period 1982-1984 = 100. It is monthly and seasonally adjusted; the not seasonally adjusted version is CPIAUCNS, on the same base. The source is the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS).

It is published jointly by the U.S. Census Bureau and the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD), from the New Residential Sales release. FRED carries it as Median Sales Price of Houses Sold for the United States (series MSPUS), quarterly, in dollars, not seasonally adjusted. It covers new single-family houses sold, not existing homes.

FRED lists the source of the main effective federal funds rate series (FEDFUNDS, monthly, and DFF, daily) as the Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System, from its H.15 Selected Interest Rates release. The rate itself is calculated by the Federal Reserve Bank of New York, which is the listed source for FRED's separate EFFR series. All are in percent, not seasonally adjusted.
